title: The Arithmetic Core: v₂(m) = 1 ↔ m ≡ 2 (mod 4)
content: The bridge that turns the whole problem from a residue question into a valuation question. For any natural m, having 2-adic valuation exactly 1 means 2 ∣ m but 4 ∤ m, which for naturals is precisely m ≡ 2 (mod 4). The proof squeezes v₂(m): `padicValNat_dvd_iff_le` says 2^n ∣ m ↔ n ≤ v₂(m), so 2 ∣ m gives 1 ≤ v₂(m) and ¬(4 ∣ m) gives ¬(2 ≤ v₂(m)); `omega` closes both directions, including the degenerate m = 0 (both sides false).

title: 2-Part Building Block: v₂(φ(2^a)) = a − 1
content: The contribution of the power of 2 dividing n. Since φ(2^a) = 2^(a−1) for a ≥ 1 (and φ(1) = 1 for a = 0, where a − 1 truncates to 0 in ℕ), the valuation is exactly a − 1. Proved by `Nat.totient_prime_pow` followed by `padicValNat.prime_pow`. This single term is what makes n = 4 (a = 2, contribution 1) a solution with no odd prime factor at all.

title: Odd Prime-Power Block: v₂(φ(p^k)) = v₂(p − 1)
content: For an odd prime p and k ≥ 1, φ(p^k) = p^(k−1)(p−1). The factor p^(k−1) is odd (a power of an odd prime), so it contributes nothing to the 2-adic valuation, leaving exactly v₂(p − 1). This is why the exponent k is irrelevant to the mod-4 question — a fact the parent's sketch ('to the first power') missed. Proved via `padicValNat.mul` and the vanishing of v₂ on the odd factor p^(k−1).
mathContext: $v_2(\varphi(p^k)) = v_2(p^{k-1}(p-1)) = v_2(p-1)$ for odd prime $p$, any $k \ge 1$.

title: Local Criterion: v₂(p − 1) = 1 ↔ p ≡ 3 (mod 4)
content: The single odd prime that keeps v₂(φ(n)) small must satisfy p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Applying the arithmetic core to p − 1: v₂(p − 1) = 1 ↔ (p − 1) ≡ 2 (mod 4) ↔ p ≡ 3 (mod 4) (using that p is odd, closed by `omega`). Primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) instead have 4 ∣ p − 1, hence v₂(p − 1) ≥ 2, and cannot appear.

title: Odd-Part Valuation as a Sum over Prime Factors
content: For odd m ≠ 0, v₂(φ m) = Σ_{p ∣ m} v₂(p − 1). Derived from Euler's product formula φ m = ∏ p^(k−1)(p−1) and `Nat.factorization_prod` (the valuation of a product is the sum of valuations); every prime factor of an odd m is itself odd, so the p^(k−1) factors drop out and each summand is v₂(p − 1). This is the odd-part half of the master split.
mathContext: $m$ odd $\Rightarrow v_2(\varphi(m)) = \sum_{p \mid m} v_2(p-1)$, each summand $\ge 1$.

title: Odd-Part Characterization: sum = 1 ⟺ m = p^k, p ≡ 3 (mod 4)
content: The decisive combinatorial step. Each summand v₂(p − 1) is ≥ 1 (odd prime ⇒ p − 1 even), so a sum equal to 1 forces the index set m.primeFactors to be a singleton: `Finset.card_nsmul_le_sum` bounds the cardinality by the sum, and nonemptiness rules out the empty (sum 0) case. A single prime factor means m is a prime power (`isPrimePow_iff_card_primeFactors_eq_one` → `isPrimePow_nat_iff`), and the local criterion forces that prime ≡ 3 (mod 4). Hence m = p^k with p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
mathContext: $m$ odd, $m \ne 0$: $\sum_{p \mid m} v_2(p-1) = 1 \iff m = p^k,\ p \equiv 3 \pmod 4,\ k \ge 1$.
relatedConcepts: sum of positive terms equal to one

title: The Master Split: v₂(φ n) = (v₂(n) − 1) + Σ_{odd p ∣ n} v₂(p − 1)
content: Isolates the prime 2. Writing n = 2^a·m with a = v₂(n) and m = ordCompl[2] n the odd part (via `ordProj_mul_ordCompl_eq_self`, `coprime_ordCompl`, `not_dvd_ordCompl`), multiplicativity of φ gives φ n = φ(2^a)·φ(m), and additivity of v₂ over the (nonzero) product combines the two building blocks into the master formula. Every term is ≥ 0, and only the 2-part term (a − 1) can vanish.

title: Main Theorem: the Corrected Characterization of v₂(φ(n)) = 1
content: The headline result. v₂(φ(n)) = 1 holds precisely for n = 4, n = p^k, or n = 2p^k with p an odd prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k ≥ 1. The forward direction feeds the master split into a finite case analysis on a = v₂(n): a ≤ 1 forces the odd sum = 1 (so n = p^k or 2p^k); a = 2 forces the odd sum = 0, i.e. no odd prime, so n = 4; a ≥ 3 makes the total ≥ 2 (impossible). The reverse direction verifies each family directly from the building blocks.
mathContext: $v_2(\varphi(n)) = 1 \iff n = 4 \ \vee\ \exists\, p\equiv 3\,(4)\ \mathrm{prime},\ k\ge 1:\ n = p^k \vee n = 2p^k$.

title: mod-4 Restatement: φ(n) ≡ 2 (mod 4) ↔ (the three families)
content: The form matching the parent's open question verbatim. Obtained from the main theorem by rewriting through the arithmetic core `padicValNat_two_eq_one_iff` applied to φ(n): φ(n) % 4 = 2 ↔ v₂(φ(n)) = 1 ↔ the three-family disjunction.

title: The Correction: n = 4 Is a Genuine Extra Solution
content: The mathematical crux of the entry. It proves φ(4) ≡ 2 (mod 4) (indeed φ(4) = 2) AND that no representation 4 = p^k or 4 = 2p^k exists with p an odd prime ≡ 3 (mod 4): such a p is odd and ≥ 3, but 4 = 2^2 and 2 have only the prime 2, so p ∣ 4 (resp. p ∣ 2) would force p ∣ 2 by `Nat.Prime.dvd_of_dvd_pow`, contradicting p ≥ 3. Hence the naive characterization 'n = p^k or 2p^k' is incomplete — n = 4 must be included, exactly as the main theorem does.
mathContext: $\varphi(4) = 2 \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, yet $4 \ne p^k$ and $4 \ne 2p^k$ for any odd prime $p \equiv 3\,(4)$.

title: Sanity Checks against Small Values
content: Concrete confirmations. Via the main theorem: n = 3 (= 3^1), n = 4, and n = 6 (= 2·3^1) all give v₂(φ(n)) = 1 (each has φ = 2). Via kernel `decide`: n = 5, 8, 15 fail φ ≡ 2 (mod 4) (their totients are 4, 4, 8, with v₂ = 2, 2, 3). These exercise all three solution families and their nearest non-solutions.
